assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clear, concrete discovery-plus-invention: trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that optical clocks reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, well beyond microwave standards. It underpins tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a future redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated it; Ye's group drove the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability. The two-name credit is compact and fair, though Ye's work also overlaps with frequency-comb and ion-clock traditions that were recognised separately.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups worldwide over two decades, with the interpretation stable and applications under way. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to separate lattice clocks from earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock recognition.
Contributions of other lattice-clock groups are not represented in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic twist angle, followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened the whole field of moire quantum matter. The impact is large, original and very rapidly adopted.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive 2011 theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery. The three-name configuration pairs theory and experiment well, although Cao and other co-authors, and other theorists, are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups and extended to many moire systems, but the nature of the superconducting pairing remains debated. The core discovery is secure, though some of the physics is still evolving.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.
Allocation between early theory, the first experiments and the follow-on moire platforms is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of a new boson consistent with the Standard Model Higgs completed the electroweak sector and is a central empirical discovery of the century. This is exactly the kind of discovery that sits at the centre of the prize.
assessment.attribution: The discovery was made by two large collaborations; the prize rule of three persons makes this hard. Della Negra, Virdee and Jenni led the original proposals and construction, and Gianotti led ATLAS at the time of the announcement. I choose three of the four credited names, but this choice is an uncertain compromise and the fourth name could reasonably replace one of them.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by both experiments and by Run 2 coupling measurements. The theoretical side was recognised in 2013, so the experimental recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit does not map cleanly onto three individuals.
Whether leadership roles or scientific contributions to the analysis should decide the allocation.
Whether the committee regards the 2013 prize as having largely closed this topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising the Hubbard model with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and then fermionic and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy, created a new platform for quantum simulation of many-body physics.
assessment.attribution: The experimental pioneers are Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger; Cirac and Zoller are theorists whose proposals, including the Jaksch-Zoller Hubbard proposal, are decisive but may be recognised under a separate quantum-simulation or quantum-information framing. Credit among experiment and theory could be tangled.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced in many labs, with quantum gas microscopes now standard. Open scientific payoff on genuinely new many-body physics is still developing, which slightly tempers urgency.
uncertainties: Whether the major physics outcome is a method or a discovery.
Overlap with the Greiner-Bloch-Haensch-era Mott insulator work and with the theory candidates Cirac and Zoller.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Observation of a diffuse flux of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos, and the association of a blazar flare and the Galactic plane with neutrino emission, opened neutrino astronomy as a new window. It is a genuine discovery grounded in a remarkable instrument.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube; Karle and Spiering were central to the design, construction and early science. The IceCube collaboration is large, and AMANDA and Baikal precursors involved others, so the credit is plausible but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is established at high significance; source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) are strong but fewer in number, and the origin of the bulk of the flux remains open. Reasonably mature, though still developing.
uncertainties: Sources of the bulk of the astrophysical flux are unresolved.
Credit relative to other neutrino-telescope pioneers is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, followed by experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells and in three-dimensional bismuth compounds, started a major subfield with deep links between topology and electronic structure.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the key theoretical proposals, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicting the HgTe case and Fu, Kane and Mele the 3D case. Molenkamp's group performed the first experiments, and Hasan's group the 3D observations. Selecting three is difficult and leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed and extended; applications are mostly still prospective. Partially overlapping with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions, so a decision needs care about the boundary.
uncertainties: The theory credit among Kane, Mele, Zhang and others is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* provide empirical access to strong-field gravity and black-hole physics, which matters to me professionally. The imaging technique and the observational result are both notable.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow, Doeleman led the VLBI development and the collaboration, and Narayan contributed key accretion theory. The result is a collaboration effort of hundreds, so a three-person configuration is a hard fit.
assessment.maturity: Imaging is robust, but quantitative tests of gravity are limited by astrophysical modelling uncertainties, and interpretation of the ring remains somewhat model-dependent. Reasonably timely but not yet fully settled.
uncertainties: Model dependence of what the images teach about gravity.
Relationship to the 2020 prize for black-hole theory and the Galactic centre.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Detection of the baryon acoustic peak in galaxy clustering gave a robust standard ruler, now a pillar of precision cosmology and of constraints on dark energy. It is an empirical result directly tied to the fundamental cosmological questions.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein et al. (SDSS) and Cole et al. (2dFGRS) reported the detection in 2005, with theoretical predictions by Peebles and Yu and by Sunyaev and Zeldovich. Credit is spread across collaborations and earlier theory, so a prize configuration is ambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across many surveys with consistent results; recent DESI hints on evolving dark energy are still being assessed but do not undermine the standard-ruler method itself.
uncertainties: Allocation relative to the theoretical predictions and to the collaborations.
Possibility that the dark-energy interpretation changes with newer data.
